en: The Birth Stories,
Book Eleven: The Section on Supporting the Mother (Mātuposakavagga)
4. The Udaya Jātaka:
“Seated alone, pure and with limbs well-restrained, having ascended the palace, she of blameless form;”
“I entreat you, O one with eyes like those of a kinnara:
let us both dwell here for this single night.
“The moat within is strewn with [bones]...”
With its firm watchtowers and battlements,
guarded by those bearing swords in hand,
this city is difficult to enter.
Neither for the young nor for the old is there any coming [into being];
then by what characteristic indeed—
"You desire union with me.
"I am a yakkha, O beautiful one;
I have come into your presence."
“Gladden me, O Blessed One;
I give you this bowl of honey.
“Whether it be a god, a yakkha, or a human...”
Do not long for another dawn beyond this one;
go on your way, O powerful Yakkha,
and having gone, do not return again.
“That delight which is the highest for those who enjoy sensual pleasures—
the cause by which beings act improperly—
may you not lose that delight, O Sucimukhī.”
“I give you a silver bowl filled with bronze.
“A man, tempting a woman with wealth,
praises her wherever he feels desire.”
“Your divine quality is contrary;
you seek it by rejecting it for a mere trifle.
“Longevity and beauty in the world of men—”
O one of beautiful form, the wealth of men diminishes; by that very same process,
your own wealth also diminishes today as you grow older.
As I observe you thus,
O illustrious princess,
your beauty is indeed fading away.
With the passing of days and nights:
‘By this very age, O wise princess Sumedhā;’
"You should lead the holy life;
you shall become even more beautiful.
"The gods do not age as humans do."
There are no folds upon their limbs;
I ask you, O powerful Yakkha,
how is the bodily form of the gods?
“Devas do not age as humans do,
nor are there wrinkles upon their limbs;
day by day they become even more beautiful.”
“Divine beauty and abundant wealth.
“Why is this multitude so afraid?
The path has been proclaimed with its many stations.”
I ask you, O powerful Yakkha:
standing where does one not fear the world beyond?
"By directing speech and mind rightly..."
Not committing evil deeds with the body,
living in a house with abundant food and drink,
being faithful, gentle, sharing, and generous;
“Being a companion, friendly, and gentle in speech—
one established in this way need not fear the next world.
“You instruct me, O Yakkha;”
As a mother, as a father—
of noble appearance I ask you:
who indeed are you, O most venerable one?
“I am Udaya, O auspicious lady;
having come here, I am attached to the agreement.
I bid you farewell, I am going.”
"I am released from your agreement.
"If you are indeed Udaya,
having come here out of attachment to the agreement..."
“Instruct me, O prince, so that there may be a meeting with you again.
“The moment of youth passes away; even so does time pass.”
There is no certainty that beings do not pass away;
the body inevitably decays.
O Udaya, do not be negligent; practice the Dhamma.
The entire earth might be filled with wealth,
belonging to one person alone and not shared by another;
yet even that he abandons, being still not free from passion.
While there is prosperity, do not be negligent; practice the Dhamma.
Mother, father, brothers, and even a wife who has been purchased with wealth—
They too shall abandon one another; therefore,
O Udaya, do not be negligent, but practice the Dhamma,
knowing that the body is but food for others.
Knowing that both the happy and unhappy states in saṃsāra are but a temporary dwelling, O Udaya,
do not be negligent; practice the Dhamma.
“Excellent is what this yakkha has spoken:
short is the life of mortals;
it is both miserable and limited.”
And that [kingdom] is joined with suffering;
therefore, I alone shall go forth into homelessness,
abandoning Kasi, the well-fortified land.
The Udaya Jātaka is the fourth.
